To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

most people place numbers linearly across the range from 1 thousand to 1 billion but place 1 million at about halfway between 1 and 1 bmillion, and that these people are more optimistic than linear number-line placings in their evaluation of largely ineffective political scenarios.
most adults in the United States do not understand large numbers in the range from 1 million to 1 trillion.

(a) the surface structure of number word labels can heavily influence people’s understanding of large numbers, (b) people who place large numbers in this way are more likely to be optimistic in their evaluations of political strategies, and (c) this effect is not due to the fact that people who place large numbers this way are less able to understand large numbers.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the cognitive mechanisms that underlie the estimation of large numbers and the implications of these mechanisms for the public understanding of large numbers.
the question of whether people have a sense of numbers that is more than a sense of number words.
the cognitive processes that underlie the comprehension of large numbers.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the number words “thousand, million and billion” are not uniformly spaced, but that people tend to believe that they are.
people who use the number line linearly are more likely to be pessimistic in their evaluation of the political situation.
there is no single best method for estimating large numbers, but there are at least two different methods, and each has its advantages and disadvantages.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the surface regularities of the number word list can have a powerful influence on people's estimates of large numbers.
the public's understanding of large numbers is not as bad as we thought it was, but it is still not as good as we might have hoped.
we found that people have a hard time dealing with numbers in the range 1 million-1 trillion and that they are often overly optimistic about the effects of political actions in this range.
The main takeaway from our work is that

people tend to treat the number words "million, billion, and trillion" like a uniformly spaced count word list, and this tendency is likely to be exacerbated when people are trying to make sense of a complex scenario.

the surface structure (i.e., the words) of numbers can heavily influence processes that deal with numbers in this large range, and it is possible that analogous surface regularity is partially responsible for parallel findings in children.
the public is not well-equipped to evaluate large numbers in the range from 1 million through 1 billion.
